Label the work email field clearly if personal addresses are not accepted, so people do not fail validation unexpectedly.
Keep a visible link to log in for returning users who land on the sign-up page by mistake.
faq: How many fields should a sign-up form have?

As few as you can manage, often just email and password, or a single social sign-in button. Every extra field gives people another reason to stop. Collect additional profile details after the account exists, when the person already has a reason to continue.
Should the sign-up form have a confirm password field?

Usually not. A show-password toggle lets people check what they typed and removes the need for a second field. If you are concerned about typos, rely on email-based password reset as the safety net rather than adding friction for everyone.
Is a terms and conditions checkbox required?

Requirements depend on your jurisdiction and what you are asking people to agree to, so check with legal advice. Often a line stating that creating an account means agreeing to the terms is used, while separate consent such as marketing emails needs its own unticked checkbox.

stats-band.intro: A stats band backs up a landing page's claims with a few large, memorable figures. Our examples show a heading with a short supporting line and four large figures with labels covering checks run, alert time, regions and teams, laid out for web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark versions.
tips: Pick three or four figures that support the page's main promise, rather than every number you can find.
Give each figure a short label that says exactly what is counted, so the number cannot be misread or overstated.
Round large numbers sensibly and use consistent units and suffixes so the row reads as a set.
Use only figures you can stand behind, and note the time period or source in small text where it matters.
faq: What numbers work best in a stats section?

Figures that prove the main benefit of the product work best, such as speed, scale, reliability or customer count. A number only persuades if the reader understands what it measures, so pair each one with a clear label and keep the set focused.
Should stats count up with an animation?

A brief count-up can draw the eye, but it is optional. Keep it short, run it once when the band scrolls into view and respect reduced-motion preferences. The final figures must be present in the HTML so search engines and screen readers get the real numbers.
How many stats should a stats band contain?

Three or four is a comfortable number for one row on desktop, and it reflows neatly into a two-by-two grid on mobile. More than that dilutes attention, and readers tend to remember only one or two of the figures anyway.

success-confirmation.intro: A success screen confirms that an action worked and shows the sensible next step. Our examples cover four workspace moments: a password reset confirmed with a sign-in button, a plan upgrade listing what is now available plus a receipt, a cancelled subscription showing access until the period ends and kept data, and a sent invite with resend, copy link and invite-more options.
tips: Say specifically what succeeded, such as the invite sent to a named address, rather than a generic Success heading.
After a password reset, send people straight to sign in, ideally with their email already filled in.
On a cancellation confirmation, state the exact date access ends, what happens to their data and how to reactivate.
After an upgrade, show the features now available and a link to the receipt, so the payment feels worth it immediately.
faq: When should you use a full success screen instead of a toast?

Use a full screen when the action is significant or ends a flow, such as resetting a password, upgrading a plan or cancelling a subscription. Use a toast or inline message for routine actions like saving, where people want to carry on without interruption.
What should a subscription cancelled screen include?

It should confirm the cancellation, give the date paid access ends, explain what happens to the account's data and offer a clear way to reactivate. Keep the tone neutral and avoid guilt-laden copy, since people who leave on good terms are more likely to return.
What should happen after an invite is sent?

Confirm who was invited and with which role, then offer useful follow-ups: resend the email, copy an invite link to share another way and invite more people. Let the person close the confirmation and return to the members list without extra steps.

team-members.intro: A team members page lets admins see who has access, what role they hold and invite new people. Our examples show a members table with roles, statuses and last-active times, seat usage and an open invite modal with email chips and a role picker, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Show seat usage next to the invite button so admins know the billing impact before they add anyone.
Let admins paste several email addresses at once and turn each into a chip, flagging invalid addresses individually.
Distinguish pending invites from active members with a status label and offer resend or revoke actions on those rows.
Default new invites to the least privileged sensible role, and describe each role briefly inside the picker.
faq: What columns should a team members table include?

Name and email, role, status such as active or invited, and last active time cover most admin needs. Add team or group membership if your product uses them. Keep row actions such as change role or remove in a menu to avoid clutter.
How should an invite flow handle multiple people?

Accept a list of emails in one field, convert each into a removable chip and apply a role to the batch with the option to adjust individually. Validate addresses as they are added, and confirm how many invites were sent once the modal closes.
How should removing a team member work?

Ask for confirmation that names the person and explains what happens to their content and access. Offer to reassign their work where relevant. Removal should take effect immediately for security, while their past activity remains attributed to them in history.

testimonials.intro: A testimonials section uses customer voices to make a product's claims believable. Our examples feature a dark featured quote card with a result metric plus two customer quotes with star ratings, names, roles and initials avatars, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles, each in light and dark themes.
tips: Choose quotes that describe a specific outcome or before-and-after change, not general praise that could apply to any product.
Attribute every quote with a name and role, since anonymous testimonials read as invented and carry little weight.
Feature one strong quote larger than the rest to give the section a focal point instead of a uniform grid.
Edit quotes for length only, never for meaning, and keep each one short enough to read in a few seconds.
faq: How many testimonials should a landing page show?

Three to six quotes is usually enough for a section, with one featured more prominently. Quality matters more than quantity. If you have many, a carousel or a link to a full customer stories page keeps the section focused without hiding the evidence.
Are testimonial carousels a good idea?

They save space, but visitors often see only the first slide, and auto-rotation can be hard to read and inaccessible. A static grid of a few strong quotes is usually more effective. If you use a carousel, give it manual controls and pause on hover and focus.
Do testimonials need photos?

Photos can add credibility, but only with permission and real customers. An initials avatar with a full name and role is a solid alternative and avoids the stock-photo look that makes readers doubt a quote. Never use stock images to represent a quoted person.

two-factor.intro: A two-factor verification screen asks for a second proof of identity after the password. Our examples show a six-digit code input with three digits entered, a resend countdown, a trust-this-device checkbox and a backup-code link, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark versions.
tips: Support pasting the full code and set the autocomplete attribute to one-time-code so phones can autofill it from a text message.
Show where the code was sent with a partly masked number or address, so people know which device to check.
Disable the resend link behind a visible countdown, then enable it, to stop repeated requests without leaving people guessing.
Always offer a recovery route such as backup codes, because losing the second factor should not lock someone out permanently.
faq: Should a 2FA code input use separate boxes for each digit?

Separate boxes look clear, but they must behave like a single field: accept paste, move focus automatically, support backspace across boxes and work with autofill. A single well-styled input with wide letter spacing is simpler to build accessibly and works just as well.
What does trust this device mean on a 2FA screen?

It lets the person skip the second factor on that browser or device for a set period, usually by storing a secure token. Say how long the trust lasts, and let people review and revoke trusted devices from their security settings.
Should two-factor screens submit automatically when the code is complete?

Auto-submitting once all digits are entered saves a step and works well for most people. Keep a visible Verify button as well for clarity and assistive technology, and show errors inline next to the input without clearing the code entirely.

welcome.intro: A welcome screen greets new users after sign-up and guides them to their first meaningful action. Our examples show a personal greeting, three getting-started choices, a five-step setup checklist with progress and a primary call to action, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark themes.
tips: Greet people by name and get to the point in one line; the screen's job is to start them doing something.
Offer a small number of starting paths, such as a template, an import or a blank start, matched to common goals.
Pre-tick checklist items the person has already completed, like creating an account, so progress starts above zero.
Make the checklist dismissible and reachable later, because some users prefer to explore before following guided steps.
faq: What should a welcome screen after sign-up include?

A short greeting, a clear first action and a way to choose between a few starting points. A setup checklist helps if the product needs several steps before it is useful. Avoid long tours on this screen; let people begin and offer help in context.
Do setup checklists help new users?

They often help because they make the path to value visible and give people a sense of progress. Keep the list short, order items by importance, and make each item link straight to the place where the task is completed.
Should a welcome screen use a product tour?

Brief, optional tours can help with unfamiliar interfaces, but many people skip them. Contextual hints that appear when a feature is first used tend to be more effective than a long tour shown immediately. Always provide an obvious way to skip.

chat-list.intro: A chat list helps people see which conversations need attention and jump into them. Our examples show channels and direct messages with unread counts, presence indicators, message previews and search, designed for a fictional team chat product on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Make unread conversations stand out with bold names and a count, and keep muted conversations visibly quieter.
Show presence with both colour and shape or a label, so status is readable for people with colour vision deficiency.
Truncate previews to a single line and include the sender's name in group conversations so context is clear.
Keep search pinned at the top of the list and let it match people, channels and message content.
faq: Should channels and direct messages be in one list or separate sections?

Separate collapsible sections work well for team chat because people think about channels and private conversations differently. A single list sorted by recent activity suits personal messaging. Whichever you choose, let people pin or star important conversations to the top.
How should unread messages be indicated in a chat list?

Use bold text for unread conversations and a numeric badge for direct messages or mentions. Plain channel activity can use a subtler dot to avoid badge fatigue. Clear the indicator as soon as the conversation is opened and read.
What information belongs in each chat list row?

The conversation name, an avatar or icon, a one-line preview of the latest message, its time and the unread state. Presence suits direct messages. Avoid adding more metadata, as the list must be scannable at a glance on a small screen.

chat-thread.intro: A chat thread is where team conversations happen, so it must stay readable as messages pile up. Our examples show a conversation with emoji reactions, a reply thread, a file attachment, a typing indicator and a message composer, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark versions.
tips: Group consecutive messages from the same sender under one name and avatar to reduce visual noise.
Insert date separators and a clear new-messages divider so people can find where they left off.
Keep the composer fixed at the bottom and grow it with multi-line text up to a sensible maximum height.
Show file attachments as cards with name, type and size, so people know what they are opening before they click.
faq: Should chat messages use bubbles or a flat list?

Bubbles suit one-to-one personal messaging, where alignment shows who said what. Flat, left-aligned lists with names suit team chat, where many people take part and messages can be long or contain code and files. Choose based on group size and content.
How should threaded replies appear in a chat conversation?

Show a compact reply summary under the original message, with participant avatars and a reply count, and open the full thread in a side panel or separate view. This keeps the main conversation readable while side discussions continue.
Where should timestamps go in a chat thread?

Show a time next to the first message of each group, and reveal exact times on hover or long press for the rest. Use date separators between days. This gives enough context without repeating a timestamp on every line.

video-call.intro: A video call screen has to keep people, controls and side information in balance during a live conversation. Our examples show participant tiles, an active-speaker highlight, mute, camera, share and leave controls and a side panel, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles, each in light and dark themes.
tips: Highlight the active speaker with a clear border or larger tile so people can follow who is talking.
Keep mute and camera buttons in fixed positions and show their state with both icon and label or tooltip.
Make Leave visually distinct from the other controls, often red and set apart, so it is not pressed by accident.
Show muted status on each participant tile, which saves people from speaking to someone who cannot hear them.
faq: How should video call controls be arranged?

Place them in a single bar at the bottom of the screen, with microphone and camera first, then sharing and secondary tools, and Leave at the end. Keep the order stable so people build muscle memory. On mobile, hide less-used tools in a More menu.
Should video call controls auto-hide?

Auto-hiding gives more room to video, but controls must reappear instantly on mouse movement, tap or keyboard focus. Keep the mute state visible even when the bar is hidden, as it is the status people check most often during a call.
How do you lay out many participants in a video call?

Use a grid that adapts to the number of people and switch to a speaker view for presentations or larger meetings. Paginate or scroll beyond a sensible number of tiles, and let people pin a specific participant to keep them visible.

map-view.intro: A map view lets people explore places spatially and compare them in a list. Our examples show an illustrated map with photo-spot pins and clusters, filters, a selected-place card and a results list on web or a bottom sheet on mobile, designed in eight visual styles with light and dark themes.
tips: Cluster nearby pins with a count when zoomed out, and expand clusters on tap so the map never becomes unreadable.
Keep the map and list in sync: selecting a pin should highlight its list item and the reverse.
On mobile, use a draggable bottom sheet with peek, half and full heights so people can balance map and results.
Offer a Search this area button after panning instead of reloading results automatically on every small map movement.
faq: Should a map screen show a list as well as the map?

Usually yes, because lists are easier for comparing details and more accessible to screen reader users. On desktop, a side-by-side layout works well. On mobile, a bottom sheet or a map and list toggle lets people switch without losing their place.
How should map pins be designed?

Pins should be distinct from the map background, show category through shape or icon as well as colour, and have a clear selected state. Keep them small enough not to obscure the map, and make the tap target larger than the visible pin.
What happens when someone taps a map pin?

Show a compact preview card with the name, a photo, key details and a primary action, without leaving the map. Tapping the card opens the full place page. Centre the map on the pin if the card would otherwise cover it.

video-player.intro: A video player page has to play content well and help viewers decide what to watch next. Our examples show a player with chapters and controls, a creator row, likes and an up-next list, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles from minimal to retro, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Mark chapters on the progress bar and show the chapter title on hover so viewers can skip to the part they want.
Make every player control reachable by keyboard and give each one an accessible name, not just an icon.
Put captions within one tap of the main controls, since many people watch with sound off.
Show duration and creator on each up-next item so viewers can judge it without leaving the current video.
faq: Which controls does a video player need?

Play and pause, a seek bar, current time and duration, volume, captions, settings for quality and speed, and full screen are the core set. Picture-in-picture and chapters are useful additions. Group the essentials and move the rest into a settings menu.
Should a video autoplay the next item?

Autoplaying the next video is common, but it should be easy to turn off and show a short countdown with a cancel option first. Autoplay with sound on page load is generally poorly received and blocked by most browsers.
How do video chapters help viewers?

Chapters break a long video into labelled sections, so viewers can scan the structure and jump straight to what they need. Show them as markers on the progress bar and as a list below or beside the player with timestamps.

create-post.intro: A create post screen guides people from picking photos to publishing them with the right details. Our examples show selected photos, a caption with hashtags, location and people tags, visibility settings and upload progress, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark versions.
tips: Start uploading photos in the background while people write the caption, so publishing feels quick at the end.
Show who will see the post right next to the Share button, because visibility mistakes are hard to undo.
Let people reorder and remove selected photos with obvious handles and a remove control on each thumbnail.
Save drafts automatically so a closed app or lost connection does not throw away a caption someone spent time on.
faq: What should a create post screen include?

A preview of the selected media, a caption field, optional tags for location and people, visibility or audience settings and a clear publish action. Upload progress and draft saving reduce anxiety, while advanced options can sit behind a More settings link.
Should visibility settings default to public?

Choose the default that matches what people expect from your product, and always show it clearly before publishing. For personal or sensitive content, a more private default is safer. Remembering the last choice is convenient but must be visible to avoid surprises.
How should hashtag and people suggestions work?

Show suggestions in a dropdown as the person types the trigger character, matching on the text so far. Insert the chosen tag cleanly and let people keep typing. Limit the list to a few relevant items so it does not cover the caption.

class-schedule.intro: A class schedule screen helps people find a session that fits their week and book it. Our examples show a week day-picker, filters and a timetable of classes with spots left, waitlist status and book buttons, designed for a fictional studio on web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark themes.
tips: Show the spots remaining on each class and switch the button to Join waitlist when the class is full.
Let people filter by class type, instructor and time of day, and remember their filters between visits.
Mark classes the person has already booked directly in the timetable so they can avoid double booking.
Make the selected day obvious in the day-picker and scroll the list to the next upcoming class for today.
faq: How should a class timetable be laid out on mobile?

A horizontal day-picker at the top with a vertical list of classes below works best on narrow screens. Each row shows time, class name, instructor, length and availability. Calendar grids that show the whole week tend to be too cramped on phones.
How should a waitlist be shown on a schedule?

Replace the Book button with Join waitlist when a class is full and show the waitlist position after joining. Explain how promotion from the waitlist works, for example whether people are booked automatically and notified, so there are no surprises.
What details should each class row include?

Start time, duration, class name, instructor, level and spots remaining are the key details. Add location or room if the studio has several. Keep descriptions on the class detail screen so the timetable stays quick to scan.

booking-details.intro: A booking details screen confirms what someone is reserving before they commit. Our examples show a class summary, a spot picker, credits used, optional add-ons, the cancellation policy and a confirm button, designed for a fictional fitness studio on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each in light and dark themes.
tips: Summarise the class, time, location and instructor at the top so people can confirm they chose the right session.
Show the total cost or credits used, including add-ons, right beside the confirm button before it is pressed.
State the cancellation window in plain words, such as free cancellation up to a set time before class, near the confirm action.
In a spot picker, show taken, available and selected spots with distinct shapes or labels, not colour alone.
faq: What should a booking confirmation step show before payment?

It should show what is being booked, when and where, the full price or credits, any add-ons, the cancellation terms and a clear confirm action. Seeing everything together lets people catch mistakes before they commit, which reduces cancellations and support requests.
Where should the cancellation policy appear?

Put a short summary close to the confirm button, with a link to the full policy. People are more willing to book when they know they can cancel, and showing the terms upfront prevents disputes about late cancellation fees later.
Should add-ons be pre-selected on a booking screen?

No. Pre-selecting paid extras is widely seen as a dark pattern and may conflict with consumer law in some regions. Present add-ons as clear, unticked options with their price, and update the total as they are chosen.

booking-confirmed.intro: A booking confirmed screen reassures people their place is secured and prepares them for the day. Our examples show the class details, add to calendar, directions, what to bring and reminder settings, designed for a fictional studio on web and mobile across eight visual styles with light and dark versions.
tips: Offer add to calendar for the main calendar apps or as a downloadable file, so the booking lands where people plan their day.
Include practical preparation details such as arrival time, what to bring and where to go on arrival.
Show how and when to cancel or reschedule, with a direct link, rather than leaving people to search for it.
Let people choose reminder timing on this screen, while the booking is fresh in their mind.
faq: What should a booking confirmation screen include?

Confirm the class, date, time, place and instructor, then add practical help: add to calendar, directions, what to bring and how to cancel. A booking reference and a note that an email confirmation is on its way also help people feel certain.
Is an add to calendar button worth including?

Yes, it is one of the most useful actions after booking, because it puts the session in the place people already plan their time. Offer the common calendar services and a standard calendar file that works with most apps.
How should booking reminders work?

Send a reminder at a sensible interval before the session, such as the day before and an hour before, and let people adjust or turn them off. Include the time, location and a cancel link so the reminder is useful on its own.

api-keys.intro: An API keys page lets developers create, review and revoke credentials safely. Our examples show keys with scopes and last-used times, a one-time key reveal, a create key action and usage limits, designed for a fictional workspace product on web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark themes.
tips: Show the full secret only once at creation with a copy button, and warn clearly that it cannot be viewed again.
Let people name each key and see its scopes, so they know which integration will break if it is revoked.
Display last-used times so unused keys are easy to spot and remove.
Mask stored keys to a short recognisable prefix or suffix, enough to match them against configuration files.
faq: Why are API keys only shown once?

Showing a secret once means the service can store only a hashed version, so a database leak does not expose usable keys. It also encourages people to put the key straight into a secrets manager. If it is lost, they create a new one.
What should an API keys table include?

Key name, a masked identifier, scopes or permissions, creation date, last used time and who created it. Row actions should include revoke and, where supported, rotate. Expiry dates are worth showing if keys can expire.
How should key revocation be designed?

Ask for confirmation that names the key and states that applications using it will stop working immediately. Revocation should take effect at once. Supporting several active keys lets teams rotate credentials by creating a new key before revoking the old one.

audit-log.intro: An audit log lets admins trace who did what, to which resource and when. Our examples show a filterable event table with actor, action, target, IP address and time, plus an event detail panel, designed for a fictional workspace product on web and mobile in eight visual styles with light and dark themes.
tips: Write actions in plain past-tense phrases, such as removed member, rather than raw internal event codes.
Show times in the viewer's time zone with the zone labelled, and reveal the exact timestamp on hover or in the detail panel.
Let admins filter by actor, action type, target and date range, and keep those filters in the URL for sharing.
Offer export in a standard format so logs can be kept or analysed outside the product.
faq: What fields should an audit log show?

Each event should record who acted, what they did, what it affected, when it happened and from where, such as an IP address or device. A detail view can show before and after values and any request metadata investigators need.
Should audit log entries be editable or deletable?

No. Audit logs should be append-only so they remain trustworthy as a record. Admins can filter, search and export entries, and older events may be archived under a stated retention policy, but individual entries should not be altered from the interface.
How should an audit log handle large volumes of events?

Use server-side filtering and pagination or infinite loading rather than loading everything at once. Encourage narrowing by date range and event type, and provide export for deeper analysis. Keep the table columns compact so many rows fit on screen.

roles-permissions.intro: A roles and permissions screen lets admins decide who can do what in a workspace. Our examples show a list of roles with member counts and a permission matrix for the selected role, designed for a fictional workspace product on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark versions.
tips: Group permissions by area, such as projects, billing and members, so the matrix reads as sections rather than one long list.
Describe each permission in terms of what a person can do, not internal object names.
Lock built-in roles like Owner from editing and explain why, while allowing custom roles to be duplicated and adjusted.
Show how many members a change will affect before saving edits to an existing role.
faq: How should a permission matrix be laid out?

Put permissions in rows grouped by area, with either one role at a time or roles as columns. Viewing one selected role keeps the screen manageable on smaller displays. Use clear checkboxes or toggles and explain any permission that implies another.
Should products offer custom roles?

Simple built-in roles such as Owner, Admin, Member and Guest cover many teams. Custom roles suit larger organisations with specific access needs. If you offer them, let admins start by duplicating an existing role rather than building from an empty set.
How do you prevent admins from locking themselves out?

Prevent removal of the last owner or administrator, and block edits that would strip the current user of permission to manage roles without confirmation. Show a clear warning explaining the consequence, and log every role change in the audit log.

integrations.intro: An integrations settings page shows which tools are connected and lets admins add or configure others. Our examples show connected and available integrations with connect buttons and a settings panel, designed for a fictional workspace product on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Separate connected integrations from available ones, and show each connection's status, owner and last sync time.
Explain what data an integration can read or change before the person starts the connection flow.
Surface broken connections prominently with a reconnect action, because expired authorisation often fails silently.
Open integration settings in a side panel so people keep their place in the list.
faq: What should an integrations settings page include?

A list of connected integrations with status and quick actions, a browsable catalogue of available ones with categories and search, and a settings view for each connection. Clear errors and reconnect prompts matter as much as the connect button itself.
How should the connect flow for an integration work?

Explain the permissions requested, send the person through the provider's authorisation screen, then return them to a settings panel to choose options such as which channels or projects to sync. Confirm success and show what will happen next.
How do you show an integration that has stopped working?

Mark it with a clear warning state, explain the cause in plain language, such as expired access, and offer a single reconnect action. Notify the person who set it up, since they often hold the required account access.

bento-features.intro: A bento feature grid presents several product features at once in tiles of different sizes. Our examples show mixed-size feature tiles, each with a short heading, a line of copy and a small product visual, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles from minimal to brutalist, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Give the largest tile to the most important feature, since tile size signals priority to the reader.
Keep each tile to one idea, with a short heading and one line of copy, so the grid stays scannable.
Use a consistent gap and corner radius across tiles so mixed sizes still read as one designed system.
Plan the mobile order deliberately, stacking tiles by importance rather than by their desktop grid position.
faq: What is a bento grid in web design?

A bento grid is a layout of rectangular tiles in varied sizes arranged into a tidy grid, named after the compartments of a Japanese bento box. It is often used on landing pages to show several features at once while giving some more emphasis than others.
How do you make a bento grid responsive?

Build it with CSS Grid using spans for larger tiles, then reduce the column count at smaller widths. On phones, tiles usually stack into one or two columns. Check the reading order and keep visuals legible, simplifying them where tiles become narrow.
How many tiles should a bento section have?

Somewhere between four and eight tiles is common. Fewer can look sparse, and more becomes hard to absorb. One or two large tiles plus several smaller ones creates a clear hierarchy without the grid feeling like a cluttered dashboard.

how-it-works.intro: A how it works section explains the path from signing up to getting results in a few clear steps. Our examples show numbered steps with small visuals and connectors between them, designed for landing pages on web and mobile in eight visual styles, from editorial to playful, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Keep it to three or four steps, each starting with a verb, so the process looks short and doable.
Number the steps visibly; connectors help, but the order should be clear without them.
Make the first step something the reader can do right now, and place the call to action straight after the last step.
Switch horizontal connectors to a vertical line on mobile so the flow still reads top to bottom.
faq: How many steps should a how it works section have?

Three is a common choice because it suggests simplicity, and four works if the process genuinely needs it. If your real process has many more steps, group them into stages rather than listing every action, and keep details for a help page.
Should each step have an illustration?

Small visuals help readers grasp each step quickly, especially simplified product snippets that show what they will actually see. Keep the style consistent across steps and make sure the text alone explains the step for people who cannot see the images.
Where should a how it works section go on a landing page?

It usually works best after the main value proposition and before pricing or detailed features. At that point visitors understand what the product offers and want to know how hard it is to start, so the steps answer the next natural question.

integrations-grid.intro: An integrations grid shows prospects that a product works with the tools they already use. Our examples show integration tiles for fictional tools with category filters and a request-an-integration link, designed for marketing pages on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Lead with the integrations your audience asks about most, and use category filters once the list grows beyond one screen.
Give each tile a name and a short line on what the integration does, not just a logo.
Keep logo tiles a consistent size with even padding so differently shaped marks look balanced.
End the grid with a request link so missing tools become feedback instead of a reason to leave.
faq: Should an integrations section use logos only?

Logos are quick to recognise, but adding the tool name and a short description improves clarity and accessibility. Each tile should also link to a page explaining what the integration does and how to set it up, which helps both visitors and search.
How should a long list of integrations be organised?

Group them into categories such as communication, storage and analytics, and offer search or filter chips. Show a curated selection first, with a link or button to view all. This keeps the section short while proving breadth.
Is it worth adding a request an integration link?

Yes. It gives visitors who do not see their tool a constructive next step and gives your team useful demand signals. Keep the form short, asking for the tool name and an optional email for updates when it becomes available.

changelog.intro: A changelog shows customers that a product is actively improving and explains what changed. Our examples show a release-notes timeline with entries tagged New, Improved and Fixed, and a subscribe option, designed for web and mobile in eight visual styles from minimal to retro, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Tag each entry as New, Improved or Fixed so readers can scan for the kind of change they care about.
Write entries around what users can now do, not internal ticket titles or code changes.
Date every release and give each entry its own anchor link so support teams can point customers to it.
Add a small image or clip for significant features, keeping minor fixes as short text lines.
faq: What should a good changelog entry include?

A date, a clear title, a tag such as New, Improved or Fixed, and one or two sentences explaining what changed and why it matters to the user. Larger features benefit from a screenshot and a link to documentation explaining how to use them.
How often should a changelog be updated?

Update it whenever users would notice a change, whether that is weekly or monthly. Consistency matters more than frequency. Grouping small fixes into a regular digest keeps the page useful without filling it with trivial entries.
Should a changelog let people subscribe?

Yes, an email, RSS or in-app subscribe option keeps interested customers informed without them checking back. Make the frequency clear and include an easy unsubscribe link. Many products also show a small badge in the app when there are unread updates.

careers.intro: A careers section helps candidates understand what working at a company is like and find a suitable role. Our examples show a culture blurb, perks, a department filter and a job list, designed for fictional companies on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Show the job list early with filters for department and location, since many visitors arrive looking for a specific role.
List location, working pattern and contract type on every job row so candidates can rule roles in or out quickly.
Describe perks concretely, such as a set number of leave days, rather than vague claims about culture.
Offer a useful empty state when a department has no openings, such as a sign-up for future roles.
faq: What should a careers page include?

A short description of the company and how it works, concrete benefits, a filterable list of open roles with location and type, and a clear application route. Salary ranges, where you can share them, and an outline of the hiring process help candidates decide.
Should salary ranges be shown on job listings?

Showing ranges is increasingly expected, and some jurisdictions now require it in job adverts. It saves time for candidates and recruiters alike. Check the rules for each location you hire in, and present ranges clearly alongside the role title.
How should open roles be organised?

Group or filter roles by department and location, and sort by most recent or by team. Each row should show the title, team, location and working pattern, linking to a full description. Keep the list on the main page rather than behind an external link if possible.

security-trust.intro: A security and trust section reassures buyers that their data will be handled responsibly. Our examples show compliance badges, a summary of security practices, an uptime snippet and a trust-centre link, designed for fictional products on web and mobile in eight visual styles, each with light and dark themes.
tips: Show only certifications and audits the company actually holds, and say what each one covers.
Describe practices concretely, such as encryption at rest and in transit and single sign-on support, in plain terms buyers can check.
Link to a trust centre or status page with fuller detail rather than cramming policies into the section.
Give security reviewers a direct contact or document request route, since they often need more than marketing copy.
faq: What should a security section on a website include?

Relevant certifications or audits, the main technical controls such as encryption and access management, data location and privacy commitments, uptime or status information and a link to deeper documentation. A contact route for security questions and vulnerability reports is also valuable.
What is a trust centre?

A trust centre is a dedicated page or site collecting a company's security, privacy and compliance information, such as policies, certifications, subprocessors and status. It helps buyers' security teams complete reviews without lengthy back-and-forth emails.
Is it acceptable to show compliance badges before certification is complete?

No. Displaying a badge implies the certification has been achieved, so showing it early is misleading. If an audit is underway, say so in plain text, for example that an assessment is in progress, and update the badge once the report is issued.

ai-workspace.intro: An AI workspace is where someone gives a model a task, checks what it produced and decides what happens next. Our screens pair an input panel with sources and options, a generated result with citations, and clear next-step actions to refine, export or share, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Keep the input, the result and the next action visible together, so people can iterate without losing context.
Show which sources the result draws on, with citations people can open, so the output can be checked.
Make generation state obvious: queued, generating, done or failed, with a way to stop a long run.
Offer specific follow-ups (shorten, add a table, change tone) rather than only an empty prompt box.
faq: What should an AI generation workspace include?

An input area with the prompt and any attached sources or settings, the generated result, the state of the run, and actions for what to do next, such as refine, regenerate, export or share. Citations or source links help people trust and verify the output.
Should the prompt panel sit beside or above the result?
On wide screens a side-by-side layout works well because people can tweak the input while reading the result. On mobile, stack them and keep the input reachable at the bottom of the screen.

ai-settings.intro: AI settings let people choose a model, connect provider API keys, cap spending and tune how an assistant behaves or sounds. Our screens show model and provider choices, masked API keys, usage meters with spend limits and voice options, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Mask API keys after they are saved and show only the last few characters, with copy, rotate and revoke actions.
Put usage and spend next to the limit that controls it, so people can see how close they are before they hit it.
Explain model choices in plain terms (speed, cost, quality) instead of listing only model names.
Group voice and behaviour options separately from billing and keys, since different people manage them.
faq: How should API keys be displayed in settings?
Show a key in full only once, when it is created. After that, display a masked version with the last four characters, its creation date and last use, plus actions to copy, rotate or revoke it.
What usage information belongs on an AI settings page?
Current usage against a monthly limit, spend so far, a simple trend, and a control to set or change the limit. Alerts at thresholds such as 80% help avoid surprise cut-offs.

version-history.intro: A version history screen lets people see how a document changed over time, compare two versions and restore an earlier one. Our screens show a timeline of versions with authors and times, a before-and-after diff with additions and removals highlighted, and a restore action, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Mark additions and removals with more than colour, such as plus and minus signs or strikethrough, so the diff stays readable for everyone.
Name versions by author and time, and let people label important ones, so the timeline is easy to scan.
Let people compare any two versions, not only a version with the current one.
Make restoring safe: restore as a new version rather than deleting the history after it.
faq: How do you show differences between two versions?
Use a side-by-side or inline diff. Highlight added text and removed text with distinct backgrounds, and add plus and minus markers or strikethrough so the change is clear without relying on colour.
Should restoring a version delete later versions?
No. Restore by creating a new version that copies the old content. That keeps the full history and lets people undo the restore.

approval-queue.intro: An approval queue collects requests that need a decision, such as access requests, expenses or content changes, so a reviewer can work through them quickly. Our screens show pending requests with filters, a selected request with its proposed changes, and approve and reject actions, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Show what is being requested, by whom and why in the list itself, so many requests can be triaged without opening each one.
Keep approve and reject next to the details of the selected request, and ask for a reason when rejecting.
Support bulk actions and keyboard shortcuts for reviewers who handle many requests a day.
Show how long each request has waited, so older requests do not get stuck.
faq: What should each request in an approval queue show?
The requester, what they are asking for, the reason or context, when it was submitted and its current status. A preview of the proposed change helps reviewers decide quickly.
Should rejecting a request require a reason?
It is good practice. A short reason tells the requester what to change and gives the team a record of the decision.

doctor-directory.intro: A doctor directory helps patients find the right clinician and book with confidence. Our screens show specialty filters, search, and doctor cards with photo placeholders, specialties, languages spoken, the next available slot and in-person or video badges, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Lead with what patients filter by most: specialty, availability, language and in-person or video visits.
Show the next available appointment on each card, so patients can book without opening every profile.
Use real photos and plain-language bios in production; a friendly, human tone builds trust.
Make the book button the clear primary action on each card.
faq: What information should a doctor profile card show?
Name, specialty, a photo, languages spoken, whether they offer video visits, and the next available appointment. Ratings, qualifications and a short bio can go on the full profile.
How should patients filter a medical team page?
By specialty first, then availability, visit type (in person or video), language and location if the clinic has several sites.

telehealth-visit.intro: A telehealth visit takes a patient from a waiting room with a camera and microphone check, into the video consultation, and out to a visit summary. Our screens show each step: device check and appointment details, the in-call view with mute, camera and end-call controls, and an after-visit summary with prescriptions and follow-up, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Let patients test their camera, microphone and connection in the waiting room before the doctor joins.
Keep call controls large, labelled and always visible, especially end call and mute.
Show appointment details and the doctor's name during the call, so patients know who they are speaking with.
End with a plain-language summary: what was discussed, prescriptions sent, and how to book a follow-up.
faq: What should a telehealth waiting room include?
A camera preview, microphone and speaker checks, the appointment time and doctor, a status message such as 'Your doctor will join shortly', and a clear join button.
What goes in an after-visit summary?
A plain-language note of what was discussed, any prescriptions and where they were sent, next steps, a follow-up booking option and billing or insurance status.

clinic-home.h1: Clinic website homepage UI design examples
clinic-home.intro: A clinic homepage has to help patients book quickly and feel reassured. Our screens show a hero with a booking entry point, a grid of medical specialties, a preview of the doctor team, opening hours and location, and accepted insurance, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Put booking and contact in the first screen; most visitors arrive wanting an appointment.
List specialties in plain language so patients can find the right service without medical vocabulary.
Show real doctors and opening hours to build trust and answer common questions up front.
Make phone numbers tappable and addresses open in maps on mobile.
faq: What should a clinic homepage include?
A clear way to book or call, the specialties offered, the doctor team, opening hours and location, insurance accepted, and whether video appointments are available.
How do you make a healthcare website feel trustworthy?

Use real people, plain language and calm, readable design, and be specific about hours, costs and how to get help. Accessibility, with good contrast and large tap targets, matters for patients of all ages.

music-player.intro: A music player's now-playing screen puts the track front and centre with the controls people use most. Our screens show album artwork, track and artist, a scrubber with elapsed and remaining time, transport controls, an up-next queue and lyrics or credits, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Keep play and pause the largest control, with previous and next on either side.
Show elapsed and remaining time on the scrubber, and make it easy to drag accurately.
Give quick access to the queue, so listeners can see and change what plays next.
Credit artists and writers on the screen; listeners often want to know who made the track.
faq: What controls should a music player have?
Play and pause, previous and next, a seek bar with times, shuffle and repeat, volume (on web), like or save, and access to the queue and lyrics.
How should a web music player differ from mobile?

On web, a three-part layout works well: library on the left, now playing in the middle and the queue on the right. On mobile, focus on the artwork and controls, with the queue and lyrics a swipe or tap away.

playlist.intro: A playlist or album screen lets listeners see what is in a collection and start playing it. Our screens show the cover, title and curator, play and shuffle buttons, and a numbered track list with durations, play counts, explicit and downloaded badges and download progress, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Put play and shuffle right under the title, so starting the playlist is one tap.
Keep track rows consistent: number, title and artist, then duration, with badges small and secondary.
Show download progress per track and overall when people save a playlist for offline listening.
Highlight the track that is currently playing in the list.
faq: What should a playlist track list show?
Track number, title, artist, duration and small indicators such as explicit, downloaded or currently playing. Album and date added are useful on wide screens.
How should offline downloads be shown?
Show a download toggle for the whole playlist, a progress indicator on tracks that are downloading, and a clear mark on tracks that are available offline.

portfolio-home.intro: A portfolio homepage should say who you are, show your best work and make it easy to get in touch. Our screens show a hero with a name, positioning and two clear paths (hire me or see the work), a selected-work index with client, year and role, services and contact, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Say what you do and for whom in one line at the top of the page.
Show a handful of strong projects rather than everything, each with client, year and your role.
Give visitors two clear paths, such as 'See the work' and 'Get in touch'.
Keep contact details on every page, not only on a contact page.
faq: How many projects should a portfolio show?
Four to eight strong, relevant projects is usually enough. Lead with the work closest to the jobs you want, and link each one to a short case study.
What makes a good portfolio hero?
Your name, a one-line description of what you do and who you do it for, and one or two clear actions. Let the work below carry the visual weight.

case-study.h1: Case study page UI design examples
case-study.intro: A case study explains a project from problem to outcome, so a reader can see how you think as well as what you made. Our screens show the project title, client, role, timeline and stack, the problem, process steps, outcome metrics, large artwork panels and a next-project link, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Open with a summary: client, your role, timeline and the result, for readers who only skim.
Explain the problem and the constraints before showing the solution.
Show outcomes with numbers where you can, and be specific about your contribution.
End with a link to the next project to keep people reading.
faq: How long should a design case study be?
Long enough to cover the problem, your process, the solution and the outcome, usually a few minutes' read. Use headings and a summary at the top so skimmers get the point quickly.
What should a case study include?
The context and problem, your role, key decisions and how you reached them, the final design, and the results. Images of the work should be large and clearly captioned.

security-dashboard.intro: A security dashboard shows a team where it is exposed and what to fix first. Our screens show vulnerabilities broken down by severity (critical, high, medium and low), an open-findings table with affected assets, a trend over time, a compliance score and recent alerts, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Order everything by severity, and make critical findings impossible to miss.
Pair severity colours with labels or icons, since colour alone is not enough.
Show the trend, not just today's count, so teams can see whether they are improving.
Link each finding to the affected asset and a clear next step.
faq: What should a security dashboard show first?
The number of critical and high findings, how they have changed recently, and the specific items that need attention now. Details such as compliance scores and lower-severity issues can follow.
How should vulnerability severity be visualised?
A donut or stacked bar works well for the breakdown, with each severity labelled and counted. Use a consistent colour scale and always include the text label.

project-tracker.h1: Project tracker dashboard UI design examples
project-tracker.intro: A project tracker gives a team a shared view of what is on track and what is slipping. Our screens show project phases with progress, a project list with progress rings and team avatars, upcoming milestones, stat tiles and an activity feed, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Show progress per project and per phase, so people can see where work is stuck.
Put owners and due dates next to each project; accountability needs names.
Flag at-risk projects with a status label as well as colour.
Keep the activity feed short and link through to the full history.
faq: What should a project tracker dashboard include?
A list of projects with status, progress, owner and due date, upcoming milestones, a few summary numbers such as on track versus at risk, and recent activity.
Progress bars or progress rings?
Both work. Rings are compact in dense lists and cards; bars are easier to compare across many rows. Always show the percentage or count as text too.

course-dashboard.intro: A learning dashboard helps students see their progress and what is due next, and helps teachers see how a class is doing. Our screens show course progress cards, learning streaks and stats, upcoming assignments, the class schedule and a student progress table, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Lead with what is due next; it is the question students open the dashboard to answer.
Show progress per course with a clear percentage and the next lesson to continue.
Use streaks and badges with care, as encouragement rather than pressure.
Give teachers a sortable student table that highlights who needs help.
faq: What should a student dashboard show?
Courses in progress with completion, upcoming assignments and due dates, the timetable for the day or week, and recent grades or feedback.
What does a teacher or LMS admin dashboard need?
A class overview with average progress, a student table with completion and last activity, assignments to mark and alerts for students falling behind.

form-wizard.h1: Multi-step form wizard UI design examples
form-wizard.intro: A multi-step form, or wizard, breaks a long form into short steps so it feels manageable. Our screens show a stepper with the current step, filled example fields, validation hints and a summary side panel on web, and one step per screen with progress on mobile, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Show how many steps there are and where the person is, with step names, not only numbers.
Ask related questions together and keep each step short.
Validate fields as people go, with specific, helpful messages next to the field.
Let people go back without losing what they entered, and review everything before submitting.
faq: How many steps should a form wizard have?
As few as the task needs, usually three to five. Group related fields, and skip steps that do not apply to the person's earlier answers.
Should a multi-step form show a summary?
Yes. A running summary on wide screens, or a review step at the end, lets people check their answers before submitting and reduces errors.

bank-onboarding.h1: Bank account onboarding UI design examples
bank-onboarding.intro: Opening a bank account online takes a welcome screen, an identity check and a clear moment when the account is ready. Our screens show each step: what you will need, a numbered progress list, identity fields with a plain explanation of why they are needed, and an account-ready screen with account details, the card on its way and next steps, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Tell people up front what they will need (ID, address, a few minutes) so they can finish in one go.
Explain why each piece of personal information is needed and how it is protected, right next to the fields.
Show progress with named steps and let people pause and come back.
End with something useful to do next, such as adding money or ordering a card, not just a success message.
faq: Why do banking apps ask for ID and a selfie?
Banks are legally required to confirm who their customers are (often called know-your-customer checks). A photo ID plus a selfie lets this happen online in minutes instead of in a branch.
How many steps should account opening have?
Keep it to the few the regulation and the product need, usually four to six short steps, with progress shown throughout. Pre-fill what you can and ask for documents only once.

product-scan.intro: A product scanner lets people point their camera at a barcode or label and get useful information back. Our screens show the camera view with a scan frame, mode switcher, zoom and flash controls and a manual-entry fallback, and a result screen with the matched product, a personal verdict, key ingredients explained in plain language and an add-to-routine action, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Frame the target clearly and tell people what the camera is looking for (barcode, label or product).
Always offer a fallback: type the code, import a photo or search by name.
Lead the result with a clear verdict for this person, then the detail that supports it.
Let people correct a wrong match quickly with a rescan or search.
faq: What should a barcode scanner screen include?
A camera view with a visible scan frame, short guidance text, flash and zoom controls, a way to switch scan modes, and a manual-entry option. Recent scans are a helpful shortcut.
How should a product scan result be laid out?
Start with the product name, image and a one-line verdict, then the reasons (ingredients, compatibility, warnings) and finally the actions, such as save or add to a list.

split-view.intro: A split view, also called master-detail, shows a list on one side and the selected item's detail on the other, so people can move through many items without losing their place. Our screens use grouped, compact list rows with hairline separators and a calm detail pane, with the list on its own screen on mobile, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Keep list rows compact and scannable: title, a short snippet and one or two pieces of metadata.
Make the selected row obvious and keep it in view while the detail changes.
Group the list by something meaningful, such as date or status.
On mobile, show the list first and open the detail as a full screen with a clear back button.
faq: When should I use a master-detail layout?
When people browse many similar items and need to look at them one by one, such as email, documents, tickets or contacts. It saves a page load for every item.
How does a split view work on mobile?
Mobile screens are usually too narrow for two panes, so the list and the detail become separate screens. On tablets, both panes can sit side by side.

canvas-editor.h1: Canvas and diagram editor UI design examples
canvas-editor.intro: A canvas editor lets people lay out ideas as connected nodes, such as a sitemap, user flow or automation. Our screens show a dotted-grid canvas with connected node cards and branch labels, a tool palette, layers, an inspector for the selected node, zoom and undo controls and live collaborators, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Keep node cards small and consistent: an icon, a title and one line of description.
Label branches on the connector lines so the logic can be read without opening each node.
Put details for the selected node in a side inspector instead of crowding the canvas.
Show zoom level, fit-to-screen and undo where people expect them.
faq: What does a diagram editor need?
A canvas that can pan and zoom, a way to add and connect nodes, a panel to edit the selected node, undo and redo, and a way to share or publish. Collaboration cues such as cursors help teams.
How should a canvas editor work on mobile?
Most people review rather than build on a phone. A read-and-comment view with pinch to zoom and a bottom sheet for the selected node works well.

floor-plan.h1: Floor plan and desk booking UI design examples
floor-plan.intro: An interactive floor plan helps people find and book a desk or room in an office. Our screens show a floor plan with available, booked and selected spaces, a floor switcher, filters for desks, meeting rooms and equipment, a date and time picker and a details panel for the selected room with its schedule and a book button, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Show availability with labels or patterns as well as colour, so the plan reads for everyone.
Let people filter by what they need (a monitor, a quiet booth, room size) before they scan the plan.
Show who else is in the office and where, for teams who want to sit together.
Keep the selected space's details and the book button next to the plan.
faq: What should an office floor plan app show?
The layout of the floor, which desks and rooms are free at the chosen time, filters for equipment and space type, a legend, and the details of the selected space with a way to book it.
How do you make an interactive floor plan accessible?
Do not rely on colour alone for availability, provide a list view of the same spaces, make each space focusable with a clear label, and keep text on the plan large enough to read.

voice-call.h1: Voice call screen UI design examples
voice-call.intro: A call screen shows who you are talking to and gives quick access to the controls you need mid-call. Our screens show the contact's picture or initials, name and role, a call timer and connection quality, mute, speaker, keypad, add person and hold controls with a clear end-call button, and on web a contact details panel with shared files and notes, designed for web and mobile across eight visual styles, light and dark.
tips: Make end call large, distinct and always in the same place.
Show the call timer and connection quality so people know the call is live.
Keep mute and speaker one tap away, with clear on and off states.
On desktop, use the extra space for context about the person, such as recent messages or shared files.
faq: What controls should a call screen have?
Mute, speaker or audio output, keypad, add a person, hold and end call. Video calls add camera on or off and screen sharing.
How should an active call appear when the user leaves the call screen?
Keep a small persistent indicator, such as a bar or floating pill with the timer and end and mute buttons, so people can return to the call or hang up from anywhere.

toast-snackbar.h1: Toast and snackbar with undo examples
toast-snackbar.intro: A toast confirms an action without stopping the person who took it. These examples show a task list right after a delete: the row is gone, a dark toast names the deleted task, offers Undo with a keyboard shortcut and counts down, and a quieter success toast sits above it. Web and mobile, eight styles, light and dark.
tips: Name the thing that changed (“Draft Q3 launch brief” deleted), not just “Done”.
Offer Undo for destructive or bulk actions, and keep the toast up long enough to use it; a countdown bar shows how long is left.
Stack toasts newest-nearest and cap the stack at two or three.
On mobile, place the toast above the tab bar so it never covers navigation, and keep it to one line plus the action.
faq: What is the difference between a toast and a snackbar?

The terms are used almost interchangeably. Snackbar usually means a toast with a single action such as Undo, placed at the bottom of the screen; toast is the general name for a brief, non-blocking message.
How long should a toast with undo stay on screen?
Long enough to read and react, typically 6 to 10 seconds for messages with an action. Pause the timer while the pointer is over the toast or it has keyboard focus.
Should errors use toasts?
Only for errors that need no input. If someone has to fix something, show the error next to the field or in a banner that stays until it is resolved.

confirm-dialog.intro: A destructive confirmation should slow people down just enough. These dialogs sit over workspace settings and confirm deleting a whole workspace: they list what will be lost, link to an export first, ask the person to type the workspace name and tick an acknowledgement, and keep the red Delete button disabled until both are done.
tips: Say exactly what will be removed and for whom, with numbers, instead of a generic “Are you sure?”.
Use the danger colour only on the destructive button, and label it with the action (“Delete workspace”), never “OK”.
Reserve type-to-confirm for irreversible, high-impact actions; for small deletes, an undo toast is kinder.
Offer the safe path, such as Export or Cancel, as clearly as the destructive one.
faq: When should I use a confirmation dialog?
For actions that cannot be undone and have a large impact, such as deleting an account, a workspace or many records. For reversible actions, act immediately and offer Undo.
Why make people type the name to confirm?
It stops muscle-memory clicks and makes sure the person knows which item they are deleting, which matters when several look alike.
Where should the destructive button go?
Keep the platform convention for button order, but make the destructive button visually distinct with the danger colour and a specific label.

side-drawer.h1: Side drawer and detail panel examples
side-drawer.intro: A side drawer opens a record without leaving the list. These examples slide a customer drawer over a data table, keeping the selected rows visible behind a light scrim: a header with status, three key figures, tabs, plan and payment details, recent activity and a sticky footer. On mobile the same content becomes a bottom sheet.
tips: Keep the list visible behind the drawer so people keep their place and can compare.
Give the drawer its own header with a close button and a link to the full page.
Put the most-used action in a sticky footer so it stays reachable when the content scrolls.
On mobile, use a bottom sheet with a drag handle instead of a narrow side panel.
faq: When should I use a drawer instead of a new page?
Use a drawer for quick look-ups and light edits where people return to the list afterwards. Use a full page for long forms or content people want to share or bookmark.
Should a drawer have a scrim?
A light scrim helps show that the drawer has focus. Non-modal drawers that let people keep working in the list can skip it.
How wide should a side drawer be?
Commonly 360 to 480 pixels on desktop, wide enough for a two-column key–value list without wrapping.

command-palette.intro: A command palette lets people jump anywhere or run any action from the keyboard. These examples open over a kanban board with a typed query and grouped results: places to jump to, actions with their shortcuts, and recent items, with the highlighted row and a footer of key hints. On mobile it becomes a full-screen search sheet.
tips: Group results (jump to, actions, recent) and show the group label, so mixed results stay scannable.
Show each action’s own shortcut so the palette teaches faster paths.
Highlight the first match and keep Enter, arrows and Escape working without the mouse.
Offer a fallback such as “Search in all docs” when nothing in the list fits.
faq: What is a command palette?
A searchable list of destinations and actions, usually opened with ⌘K or Ctrl+K, that lets people navigate and act without hunting through menus.
What should a command palette show before typing?
Recent items and the most common actions, so it is useful even with an empty query.
Is a command palette accessible?
It can be: use a combobox pattern with a listbox of options, move focus with arrow keys, announce the active option and close on Escape.

date-range-picker.intro: A date range picker should make common ranges one click and custom ranges easy. These examples open over a revenue report with presets, two months with the selected range highlighted, start and end date fields, the number of days and a compare-to-previous-period toggle. On mobile, one month sits in a bottom sheet with preset chips.
tips: Lead with presets (last 7 or 30 days, quarter, year to date); most people never need the calendar.
Show two months on desktop so ranges that cross a month boundary are easy to pick.
Mirror the selection in editable text fields and show the length of the range.
Mark the start and end differently from the days in between, and do not rely on colour alone.
faq: Should a date range picker use one calendar or two?
Two side-by-side months work best on desktop because many ranges cross a month boundary. On mobile, one scrolling month in a sheet fits better.
Do I need an Apply button?
For reports that reload data, yes: it lets people adjust both dates before anything changes. For lightweight filters, apply on selection.
How do I make a date picker accessible?
Let people type dates in the text fields, support arrow-key navigation in the grid, and label each day with its full date.

form-validation.intro: Good validation tells people what went wrong and how to fix it. This create-workspace form is shown after a failed submit: an error summary links to each problem, invalid fields carry the danger colour plus an icon and a written message, a taken URL comes with alternatives, password rules show which are met, and valid fields are ticked.
tips: Put an error summary at the top after submit, with each problem linking to its field.
Write messages that say how to fix it (“Add a number”), not just what is wrong (“Invalid password”).
Never rely on colour alone: pair the danger colour with an icon and text, and keep the label visible.
Validate on blur or submit, not on every keystroke, and confirm valid fields quietly.
faq: When should form validation happen?
Check formats when a field loses focus and everything again on submit. Avoid showing errors while someone is still typing their first attempt.
Where should error messages go?
Directly below or beside the field they belong to, plus a summary at the top of the form after a failed submit so screen-reader and keyboard users can find every problem.
Should the submit button be disabled until the form is valid?
Usually not: a disabled button gives no reason. Let people submit and then show clear errors.

auth-error.intro: Sign-in fails more often than it succeeds on the first try, so the error states deserve design. These examples re-render the real sign-in and two-factor screens with their failure states: a wrong password with the attempts left, a temporarily locked account with a reset path, and an expired two-factor code with a resend action, each with an alert and the field at fault marked.
tips: Say what happened and what to do next in the same alert: attempts left, when to retry, or a reset link.
Avoid revealing whether the email exists; “Incorrect email or password” is safer than “No account found”.
Mark the field at fault with an icon and text as well as the danger colour, and keep the typed email.
For lockouts, show when sign-in reopens and offer password reset as the way out.
faq: What should a wrong password error say?
Keep it short and actionable: the email or password is incorrect, how many attempts remain, and a link to reset the password.
Should I lock accounts after failed logins?
A short, time-based pause after several failures slows down guessing without locking people out for good. Tell them how long it lasts.
How do I show an expired two-factor code?
Explain that the code timed out, keep the input visible and offer to resend or use a backup code.

payment-declined.intro: When a payment fails, people need to know nothing was charged and how to finish the order. These checkout examples show a declined card: an alert in the payment section with the reason, the card field marked with an icon and message, other ways to pay still visible and the Pay button ready to retry, on web and mobile in eight styles.
tips: Say that nothing was charged; it is the first thing people worry about.
Give the reason when you can (insufficient funds, expired card) and the next step (another card, another method).
Keep the rest of the form filled in so only the payment needs to change.
Place the error next to the payment fields, not only in a toast that disappears.
faq: What should a card declined message say?
That the payment didn’t go through, that nothing was charged, the reason if the bank gave one, and what to do next, such as using another card.
Should the checkout form be cleared after a decline?
No. Keep contact, shipping and delivery choices so people only change the payment method.
Where should payment errors appear?
Inline in the payment section, close to the card fields, and announced to screen readers with role=alert.

pro-directory.intro: A home-services directory has to answer three questions fast: who can come, when, and what it will cost. These examples show plumbers near one address with service, day, rate and must-have filters, pro cards with licence badges, rating, jobs done and reply time, hourly rate plus call-out fee, bookable arrival windows and a map with price pins. Web and mobile, eight styles, light and dark.
tips: Show the next bookable arrival window on every card; availability decides most bookings.
Put the full price model on the card (hourly rate plus call-out fee) so nobody is surprised at checkout.
Make trust signals specific and checkable: licensed, insured, background-checked, jobs completed.
On mobile, keep filters as chips above the list and move the map behind a toggle.
faq: What should a service provider card show?
Name and business, rating with review count, the price model, the next available window, trust badges and one clear book action.
Should the directory include a map?
On web, yes: a map with price pins helps people judge distance and travel time. On mobile, a list first is usually faster.

service-booking.intro: Booking a visit means describing the problem and picking an arrival window. These examples show service chips, a description with photos, a day strip, two-hour arrival windows with booked ones struck through, the address and access notes, and a summary with the call-out fee and labour estimate. The slot-taken variant shows the unhappy path: the chosen window was booked by someone else, with the next free windows suggested and the details kept.
tips: Use arrival windows, not exact times, and say how long they are.
Ask for photos; they let the pro bring the right parts.
Keep the estimate visible next to the form, and say when payment happens.
If a slot is taken mid-booking, keep everything the person typed and suggest the nearest free windows.
faq: How do I handle a time slot that gets taken during booking?
Show an alert naming the window that was taken, strike it through, highlight the next free windows and keep the rest of the form filled in.
Should customers pay upfront for home services?
Many services charge after the job, with an estimate shown upfront; say which clearly next to the confirm button.

job-tracker.h1: Job tracker examples (pro on the way, job done)
job-tracker.intro: After booking, people want to know when the pro will arrive and, afterwards, what was done and what it cost.
